segments.text: Hello, Margaret, have a seat. I've been looking over the letter from your last visit, where we started the hormone patch. It's been about three months, I believe?
Exactly twelve weeks yesterday. I wrote it down. I brought my diary, if that's useful, I've been tracking everything since the first day.
That's more than useful, thank you. Why don't you tell me how it's gone, and then we'll go through the diary together.
Well, overall, better. The main thing is the hot flushes. Before the patch I was having about eight a day, and now I'm down to about three a day.
Eight down to three. That's a big change. How would you describe them now, compared to before?
Shorter, and less intense. Before, I'd be drenched and have to change my shirt at work. Now it's more a warm wave, over in a minute or two.
That's good to hear. Tell me about the patch itself, how are you finding using it?
Fine. It's the combined patch, estradiol and norethisterone. 50 micrograms. I change it twice a week, Monday and Thursday, without fail.
Twice a week, Monday and Thursday. And you've stuck with it every time?
Yes, regularly. Well... that's what I'd like to say. Honestly, looking at the diary, there are three Thursdays last month where I wrote 'forgot'. I changed it on Friday instead.
I appreciate you telling me that, and I'm glad you wrote it down. So you've mostly used it on schedule, with a few late changes.
Yes, about three late changes last month, and perhaps a couple the month before. I can't give you the exact number, I only started marking it after the first month.
That's fine, no judgement. What tends to be going on when you forget?
Thursdays are my long days at the lab. By the time I'm home, I've forgotten.
I see. Does the patch stay on well otherwise, in the shower and so on?
Mostly, yes. It lifts at the corners in the bath, but I press it down.
Good. Any bleeding or spotting since you began? Anything like that?
Nothing unexpected. A light bleed in the first month, which you said to expect. Nothing since.
Okay. Now I'd like to ask about your general health. Is there anything else you're being treated for?
Only the low bone density, osteopenia, they called it, found on my scan two years ago. And I get migraines occasionally.
Thank you. Let me take your measurements while we talk. Blood pressure is 118 over 74.
And your weight is 66 kilograms, which is the same as last time, I see.
Yes, I weighed myself this morning too. I'm quite consistent about it.
Any trouble with your heart lately, chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath on the stairs?
No, nothing. My heart feels normal. I climbed the stairs at the lab four times yesterday without a problem.
Good. Now I'm going to listen to your chest, so breathe in and out slowly for me.
Your chest is clear. Now let me check your calves, since you're on estrogen. They're soft and not tender, with no swelling.
Excellent. May I ask my question now? I wrote it down. I read an article saying hormone therapy raises the risk of blood clots. Should I be on this at all, and for how long?
That's a very fair question, and the honest answer depends on your own situation. What was it that worried you most about the article?
The clots, mostly. And I'm forty-nine, so is that too young or too old for this?
At forty-nine, benefits generally outweigh risks for many women, especially with your bone density. A patch carries a lower clot risk than tablets.
So the patch is safer than pills.
For clots, yes. We'd review it each year, and there's no fixed stop date.
All right, I'll note that. Is it okay that I've been late on a few changes?
A few late changes won't harm you, but a steady level keeps the flushes down. Could you set a reminder on your phone for Thursday afternoons?
Yes, I'll set a recurring alarm for two o'clock, and I'll keep a spare patch in my bag at the lab.
That sounds perfect. Based on your diary, this looks like menopausal flushes that are responding well to the patch.
So it's working. I think I'll note that down too.
Yes. I'd like to see you again in three months, to check your blood pressure and how things are going.
Three months. I'll book it at the desk on my way out. Thank you for taking my diary so seriously, doctor.
It's the best thing a patient can bring. Take care now, Margaret.
